Do you have Thunderbird set to automatically show remote content? This option is found at <Settings | Privacy & Security | Mail Content | Allow remote content in messages>?

Thunderbird can only render the content of what's actually in the message, and unfortunately, many emails contain invalid web (HTML) code or formatting. Some readers are more strict or lax than others at glossing over those errors - maybe Thunderbird is one of strict ones.

Many or most HTML emails also include a plain-text version, and code in the email separates the two versions. It could be that the separator is incorrect and Thunderbird can't distinguish between the two and so displays them as one.

This is all a long-winded way to say that there may not be anything you can do. But try switching the message view between "Original HTML", "Plain HTML" and "Plain Text" and see if you like the appearance better. This setting is found at menu option <View | Message body as>. By "email provider" I mean, do you get your email from, say, Gmail, Yahoo, Comcast, Charter, etc? Most or all email hosts have a web mail page that lets you read and send mail using only a web browser. So you should go to that page and check out the Spam folder there. Thunderbird (and all POP mail clients) only synchronize with the Inbox folder. That means, if the server has decided a message is Spam and puts it in a Spam folder, Thunderbird will never know about it. This is one of the advantages of IMAP over POP - IMAP synchronizes all folders.

There may be a way to either turn of the spam protection on the server (so Thunderbird can take care of it) or to "whitelist" certain senders, which is what their advice to you in your initial post was about. But we'll save that for later...

So, check the Spam folder on web mail (not in Thunderbird).

content:
When someone sends an email to you a few things could happen, assuming yours is a POP account...

Scenario 1: It's received by your email provider (Earthlink?) and placed in your Inbox on the mail server out there on the Internet. Thunderbird on your local computer will check the server Inbox, and ONLY the Inbox, and if it finds new messages there, it will download them to your local computer and delete them from the server, leaving the only copy on your computer. That copy will be found in Thunderbird's Inbox, or possibly in one of its other folders. You should check all local folders (you can use Thunderbird's Search features to do this more easily.)

Scenario 2: It's received by your email provider (Earthlink?), who decides it's spam, and moves the message to their Spam folder. Since Thunderbird checks ONLY the server's Inbox for new messages, not its spam folder, Thunderbird will not know it's there and won't download it. The only way to see the message is to go to Earthlink's web mail.

Scenario 3: The sender sends the message, but there's a problem delivering it to Earthlink. The problem might not necessarily be Earthlink's - there are many points of possible failure between sender and recipient. What's supposed to happen is that the sender's mail server will keep trying to deliver it for up to several days or more, and if it keeps failing, the sender should eventually receive a non-delivery notice, but it may not happen right away.

Scenario 4: Earthlink, or someone else in the chain could be misconfigured or malfunctioning and silently rejecting the message. This isn't supposed to happen... but it sometimes does.


What this all means is that if you are receiving all other email except from this one sender, and you have searched all your local Thunderbird folders, and have checked all folders in your Earthlink web mail, then I can confidently say the message was never received.

I don't think this is a Thunderbird issue. Your next step would probably be to contact Earthlink's tech support.

Unsubscribing may not be a good idea. Anyone who would send you a virus is unscrupulous to begin with and isn't likely to honor your request. Instead, you've confirmed that yours is a valuable valid address that they can keep using and can sell to others for profit. But too late now!

You should be sure to mark those messages as Junk (keystroke "J") which will help train Thunderbird's Bayesian spam filter to recognize spam. That's a long-term solution because it takes some time for it to learn. Here's an article all about the filter:

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/thunderbird-and-junk-spam-messages

As for the short term, read the section titled "Create filters manually". If the spam is consistently from the exact same address you may be able to create a Message Filter that will automatically mark it is spam or delete it. This is generally less effective because spammers usually change addresses every time, but it can help in some situations.

content:
Here is some information supplied by the email account provider:

When creating a new folder, the server shows error: "{imaps} Bad flag in APPEND command: Nonjunk"

The error is clear — the IMAP server is rejecting the APPEND command because Thunderbird is sending two junk-related flags simultaneously:

$notjunk — a valid IMAP keyword flag NonJunk — a non-standard flag (no backslash prefix) that the server doesn't accept

This is a Thunderbird-side behavior — it's sending both $notjunk and NonJunk together when moving messages to newly created folders, and the server's IMAP parser rejects NonJunk as invalid.

If these are correct, you may need to re-authenticate, which Google forces us all to do every once in a while. To do that,

content:
No. You use your regular password everywhere, both with webmail AND in Thunderbird, when prompted. The difference is that Thunderbird won't store your password on your computer, but instead it will store a record (the token) of having authenticated you. Remember that the token is not a password, per se, and you will never need to know it.

But if you DO decide to change your password on AT&T or Yahoo, you may need to delete the tokens saved in Thunderbird's Saved Passwords, after which you will be prompted to authenticate anew... with your new password. Once you're authenticated, a brand new token will be set.
creator: rednoise

content:
The answer is, "No." Yahoo, Gmail, and many other email providers authenticate you using OAuth2. What happens is when Thunderbird first contacts Yahoo to send or receive email, it will ask for your Yahoo password. It will then set what's known as a "token" in your Saved Passwords, which appears as a seemingly-arbitrary string of characters and is NOT your actual password. The token indicates that you have been verified as you on that particular machine with your correct password. This is considered to be far more secure than the old plain password authentication method.

According to this article, AT&T also uses OAuth, but I have no personal experience with it:

https://www.att.com/support/article/email-support/KM1240462/

Here's an article that describes OAuth2 in good detail:

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/tb-oauth

content:
There are at least two factors here.

- There is no version of Thunderbird that runs on iOS, so you will need to find another email app that can do IMAP and SMTP mail, which are the standard Internet email protocols. I don't use Apple products, so I can't recommend one, but I know they're out there. When you find one, set it up to use IMAP, not' 'POP3.

- The email program on your PC (Thunderbird, I presume) should also be set up as an IMAP account, not POP3.

If all devices that talk to your email server are using IMAP, they will all synchronize with each other and all will show the same emails. If any one of them is using POP3, they will likely get out of sync and create confusion.


The article below discusses IMAP and how it is an advantage in a situation like yours:

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/imap-synchronization

Interesting. inotify is a Linux feature that monitors certain file system errors. But Windows has no such feature or program, so it cannot have any relevance to your local system. If you google "inotify initialization error" you'll find lots of discussions about it, many having to do with mail servers, so apparently it's a common configuration issue.

I guess the message you're seeing doesn't necessarily say that there's a problem with the server's file system, only that its monitoring system is unable to start. This is usually a configuration issue on their end. There's nothing you can do about it - it's out of your control.

content:
So, you want to use the account you just set up with the email address you indicated, but you want the messages you send to have a different "friendly" name than what you originally used, right? That can be changed to anything you like at any time. Go to <Account Settings | (the account in question) | Default Identity | Your Name> - change that to whatever you want. This is your default Identity and by default all new messages will show that name.

You can also set up multiple identities that can have various other friendly names, and you can choose from them when you create a message. Here's an article that goes into detail about that feature:

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/using-identities

You can also edit the "From" name on the fly when you're in the message creation window by choosing "Custom From Address" from the From drop-down list.

There's no built-in way to do that, and it wouldn't be a good idea for most people, since the filters run in the order they're listed, and if the order is changed they may not produce the desired results.

If you're handy with a text editor and careful, a plain-text filters rule files, "msgFilterRules.dat" can be found in your Profile, a separate one for each email account. This probably wouldn't be any faster than using the Thunderbird interface unless you used some fancy macros or scripting in the editor.

You do get an error for mail.mediacombb.net. However, your server settings use imap.mediacombb.net, and smtp.mediacombb.net respectively. So obviously there is a mismatch, which may be part of the problem. I don't know which server name is correct, you'll have to check with MC.

Beyond that, the certificate for imap.mediacombb.net is a mess. It uses outdated TLS versions, and is vulnerable to certain attacks. See https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/analyze.html?d=mail.mediacombb.net

Thunderbird does not accept TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 by default. Starting with Thunderbird version 78, support for TLS 1.0 and 1.1 was deprecated and disabled for security reasons, making TLS 1.2 the minimum required version.

If I were you I'd find a new email provider who know what they are doing.

- For versions prior to 15x.x, you need to make sure that Cookies are allowed (see <Settings | Privacy & Security | Web Content | Accept cookies from sites>. Optionally, delete any stored cookies for Gmail (see <Settings | Privacy & Security | Web Content | Accept cookies from sites | Show cookies>) and delete any saved passwords for that user name (see <Settings | Privacy & Security | Passwords | Saved Passwords>).

Then quit and restart Thunderbird. When it next tries to fetch or send email, you should be prompted for your credentials as usual.


- For versions 15x.x and newer, you may need to check similar things in your default web browser, that is, make sure cookies are allowed and remove any existing cookies related to Gmail. (This is my understanding - I haven't had to do this yet.)

content:
I think that your problem is a corrupt prefs.js file in your Thunderbird (TB) profile. In the startup window in your screen shot there are no accounts and no folders displayed in the folder pane on the left. This typically happens when the prefs.js gets damaged because of Thunderbird or computer crashes or power failure. When this happens TB renames the damaged prefs.js file in prefs-1.js (or invalidprefs.js) and creates a new virgin prefs.js file containing only default settings but no account settings.

I can reproduce your TB startup page by removing the prefs.js file from my TB profile folder, then starting TB (see image).

To verify whether my supposition is correct please start TB, go to Help > Troubleshooting information > Profile Folder > Open in Finder, then exit TB. In the profile folder search for the prefs.js file and look up its size (6 to 7 kB?). Then search for a much bigger prefs-1.js (or prefs-x.js) file with a recent time stamp.

Thunderbird is what is called an e-mail client application. It connects to e-mail accounts that are hosted elsewhere (Google, Microsoft, Apple, internet service providers, et al.) It is not possible to create a brand new e-mail account/address in Thunderbird. The account/address must exist somewhere else already. Thunderbird is free.

Thunderbird Pro, a paid service under development, will offer Thunderbird e-mail addresses and use a new e-mail service ("Thundermail" or "Thunderbird Pro", I'm not sure. The name may have been changed recently.). As you saw, if you are interested in getting a brand new Thunderbird e-mail address, you must put your name on the waiting list.

So, no, you cannot get a new e-mail account/address associated with Thunderbird now. Maybe soon. And it will be part of a paid service.

You can, however, get a new e-mail account/address from Google, Microsoft, Apple, Fastmail (my recommendation, paid) and other services, set up that account in Thunderbird, and use Thunderbird to receive, send, and store messages.

Po tom, co puvodni instalace z cca 2024 havarovala, jak jsem psal, jsem instaloval aktualni pred dvema mesici. Pocitac (TB) nechavam offline abych nemenil data. Snazim se dosahnout funkcnosti vcetne lokalnich Sent Draft, protoze na serverech u pop3 predpokladam nejsou.

Poljos: Vice se mi libi import, predpokladam ze zkontroluje nebo opravi neco. Nejakou zalohu mam jeste z verze 142, nebo podobne. Jsou to vzdy verze po roce 2024, predpokladam. Instaloval jsem vicekrat jak pres Flatpak, ktery se mi nelibi, protoze presunul profil a pak nektere veci nefunguji - odkazuji na puvodni user/.Thund, misto profilu ve var/app/. Zkousel jsem Betterbird - taky nepomohlo. Nerobi mi problem TB odinstalovat, nechat vyhledat tb na disku a odmazat - tim snad se dostanu k "Cistemu PC". No a zacinam odznova. Jak jsem napsal, slozky Sent a Draft maji velikost kB az stovky MB. Odmazaval jsem soubory msf, nechal opravovat, ale data se neobjevila. Prohlizecem ktery pouze prohlizi textovy soubor beze zmeny, vidim obsah zminenych slozek, ale nemaji stejnou strukturu jako v Inbox. Chybi napriklad na zacatku X-Account-Key:, X-UIDL: Nevim, co je dulezite, tak nevim co hledat. Po mnoha pokusech a hledanich jsem se rozhodl zkusit zeptat. A doufam v pozitivni vysledek.

Nejdříve bych ověřil, že Thunderbird skutečně používá profil, který jsi zkopíroval. Píšeš, že jsi profil přenesl importem nebo kopírováním. To jsou dvě různé věci a není jasné, kterou jsi nakonec použil.

Mohl bys napsat: Jakou cestu ukazuje Nápověda → Informace pro řešení problémů → Adresář profilu? Jakou velikost mají soubory Sent a Drafts (bez přípony) v adresáři Mail/...? Jsou tyto soubory opravdu ve stejném profilu, který Thunderbird používá?

Pokud mají soubory bez přípony desítky MB, e-maily v nich s velkou pravděpodobností stále jsou. Soubory .msf jsou pouze indexy a jejich případné smazání data neodstraní – Thunderbird je vytvoří znovu.

Ještě jedna otázka: když otevřš soubor Sent (bez přípony) v obyčejném textovém editoru, vidíš v něm text typu From:, Subject: a Date:? Pokud ano, jsou zprávy stále fyzicky uložené.

Por seguridad, muchos servidores bloquean el envío de archivos .eml porque pueden contener código ejecutable. content:
Thunderbird does not have "an account" as is the case with many mail clients, it has incoming accounts and outgoing accounts and they are linked via the identity information on the incoming account (there is also no limit on the number of distinct identities you can have on and incoming account.)

I therefore really do not follow your line of thought. There is no limit to the number of SMTP servers that can be configured and each can have it's own used name and password. The SMTP to be used with an identity is set in the account settings for the incoming account on the identity pane (the one above server settings)

Check the outgoing server(SMTP) entry in account settings for configured outgoing servers and add whatever you need.

content: With IMAP all mail is managed on the server. The IMAP client, i.e. Thunderbird, is just like a mirror of what's on the server. The IMAP server did delete your restored local backup, because it knew nothing about it. This isn't a bug, it's just how IMAP works. Therefore you need to restore the backup to your Local Folders account. Then you can upload the restored messages to the IMAP server. Email servers are not made for mass transactions and may limit the amount of data and/or no. of messages being transferred. So copy your messages to the server in smaller badges, and no all at once.

content:
If yours was a POP account, messages in the Archive folders are local to your computer, though still listed among the Spectrum folders. They will be accessible, but I recommend that you move them all to the Local Folders pseudo-account. That way you can eventually delete Spectrum from your accounts in Thunderbird and your archives will be out of the way and safe and accessible.

If yours was an IMAP account, and your Spectrum account is still active, it's possible that when they shut you off (or you shut them off) the Archive folder(s) might become inaccessible. To avoid this, copy anything you want to keep into Local Folders. Then, when you're ready, you can delete the Spectrum account from Thunderbird.

In other words, anything in the Local Folders hierarchy is on your computer and unaffected with any other on-line email account.

Please consider making regular backups of your Thunderbird profile. That include all your carefully archived local messages.

content:
Yes, it could be an issue. As you noticed. you're warned to not use the Export Profile feature if your profile is over 2 GB. I've never used that feature myself, instead I manually back it up. Here are some instructions on how to do that in a Windows system:


- With your operating system's filer browser, go to the Thunderbird Profile folder. The default location for various operating systems are: 

   Windows: C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Thunderbird\Profiles\    macOS: ~/Library/Thunderbird/Profiles/    Linux: ~/.thunderbird/

- Close Thunderbird completely.

- Create, in a convenient place, a folder to contain your backup.

- Copy the entire profiles folder.

- Paste it into the folder you just created.

- Optionally, compress the folder you just pasted with a file compression utility to ZIP, 7ZIP or other format .


An alternative is the add-on "ImportExportTools NG", which has a good Export Profile feature.

content:
There is no further step you should need to take. The PROFILES.INI file tells Thunderbird where to find your default profile during startup.

When you copy a folder over another folder with the same name, and they both contain files of the same name, Windows will always warn you and ask what you want to do. In this case, both the .\Thunderbird folder from the old computer AND the .\Thunderbird folder on the computer should contain the files PROFILES.INI and INSTALLS.INI . That will trigger the overwrite warning. If they don't, one or both of those folders are incomplete. You should check both folders for the presence of those files. And examine the content of those files with Notepad or other text viewer. After the copy operation, the one in the target folder will, of course, be the same as the one in the source folder. If they are different, your copy operation was not successful.

For example, this is the content of the .\Thunderbird folder on my Windows 7 computer:

11/01/2025 05:20 PM <DIR> . 11/01/2025 05:20 PM <DIR> .. 11/01/2025 05:20 PM <DIR> Crash Reports 11/01/2025 05:20 PM 71 installs.ini 11/01/2025 05:20 PM <DIR> Pending Pings 11/01/2025 05:20 PM <DIR> Profiles 11/01/2025 05:20 PM 293 profiles.ini

content:
Thunderbird by default does not allow remote content to be displayed, so assuming you have not changed that setting then downloading and opening email will not cause a problem.

However, if you click on links in emails without checking out what the real link is first then you may open an unsafe webpage in a browser which can force an auto download of bad file. check all links before you choose whether it's ok to click on them - hover over link to see real link in bottom Status bar.

Be wary of attachments - nefarious people will try to get you to open attachments because they are banking on you being too curious for your own good. eg: Here is your Invoice attached, so you think what invoice and promptly open the pdf. However, it;s not a real pdf, it's an exec file for something you do not want. Never allow curiosity to get the better of you. If you have not bought anything and do not expect Invoice then it isn't. Some people pretend they already have your passwords and access to your computer and they want money. The odds are on that they do not, they are scarmongering hoping to extract monies under false pretences. Do not open attachments if they are not expected or you are not sure of sender. It might use a friends email address, but does that emails sound like it's from that person. When in doubt, email or ring person to ask if it's from them.

If you think it's a bad one, delete the email and compact the folder it was in, then empty the Trash and compact trash. Compacting removes all traces of deleted and moved email from within Thunderbird profile files.

I would also advise clear your cache as well. In Thunderbird

  • Settings > General
  • Scroll down to 'Disk Space'
  • click on 'Clear Now'

If desired you could select checkbox 'clear cache on shutdown'

I should also advise you clear cache in your browser as well.


Advice on running scans. Exit all programs Restart computer in 'Safe Mode' only so no internet connectivity and operating only basics. Run full scans OR select to scan specfic folders eg: temp

It's also possible the AV found a false positive, but better safe then sorry.

In Thunderbird

  • Settings > Privacy & Security
  • Security section
  • Antivirus
  • checkbox ' Allow antivirus clients to quarantine individual incoming messages':

By default, Thunderbird stores each mail folder locally as single mbox file. For example, there's a file called 'Inbox'. If your antivirus software detects a virus in a new incoming message, it will quarantine the entire inbox file because the new message has been saved to that file. That may not be convenient as the Inbox mbox file may have a lot of emails in it.

But with this setting enabled, Thunderbird first stores each incoming message in a temporary file in the system temp folder on your computer, allowing your antivirus software to only quarantine a single message. If the file is removed by the antivirus, then you get an error message about the file being missing. If the new message file still exists after being scanned by antivirus software, then it is moved to your Thunderbird inbox folder file.

content:
Not sure what you mean by "maps", but there seems to be a number of possible causes of the "phantom folder" issue, and just as many possible solutions. Some of them are:

- Right-click on the account name in the Folders List and click the "Refresh" button. If the phantom folders still show up, untick the box for any folders you don't want to see.

- Go to <Accounts Settings | Server Settings | Advanced button> . Uncheck the "Server supports folders that contain sub-folders and messages" option and see if that gets you the result you want.

- Some people report that if you delete the sub-folders first, you can then delete their containing folder.
